passage.title: The New Boy
paras: When Mr. Saleh moved the new student, Yusuf, into the seat beside Hassan, Hassan sighed loudly. He had saved that seat for his best friend all year. Yusuf had arrived from Sudan two weeks earlier. He spoke Arabic with an accent the class found funny, and he hardly ever smiled.
“He thinks he is better than us,” Hassan told his friends at break. “He never laughs at our jokes.”

For days, Hassan pretended not to notice when Yusuf dropped his pencil or searched for the right page. Then, one afternoon, the class was given a group project on rivers of Africa. Hassan was paired with Yusuf. He was reluctant, but he had no choice.

Yusuf knew everything about the Nile. He described how the Blue Nile and the White Nile meet at Khartoum, and he drew the meeting point from memory. As he drew, his face changed. “My father used to take me there on Fridays,” he said quietly. “He is still in Khartoum, in the hospital. We could not bring him.”

Hassan put down his pen. He thought about all the jokes, and about how he had assumed that silence meant pride. The next morning he arrived early and left a small gesture on Yusuf’s desk: a hand-drawn map of the school, with the canteen, the library and Hassan’s own house marked in red. At the bottom he had written, “In case you get lost. I live near here too.”
Yusuf read it twice. Then, for the first time, he smiled.

items.stem: Why does Hassan resent Yusuf at the beginning of the story?
options: Yusuf has taken a seat that Hassan was saving for his friend.
Yusuf has told the teacher that Hassan was being unkind.
Yusuf has laughed at Hassan’s jokes in front of the whole class.
Yusuf has refused to work with Hassan on the project.
items.skill: Explains character motivation

items.stem: What does Hassan assume about Yusuf’s silence?
options: that it shows Yusuf is ill
that it shows Yusuf is shy
that it shows Yusuf is proud
that it shows Yusuf is sad
items.skill: Makes inferences from literary text

items.stem: Which event is the turning point of the story?
options: Hassan tells his friends that Yusuf thinks he is better.
Yusuf explains that his father is in hospital in Khartoum.
Mr. Saleh moves Yusuf into the seat beside Hassan.
Yusuf reads the map twice and then smiles at last.
items.skill: Identifies the climax or turning point

items.stem: What does the hand-drawn map show about Hassan?
options: He wants Yusuf to visit the hospital in Khartoum.
He wants Yusuf to find a different seat in class.
He wants to show the class how well he can draw.
He wants to welcome Yusuf and offer him friendship.
items.skill: Analyzes how a character’s actions reveal change

items.stem: Which sentence BEST states a theme of the story?
options: New students should try harder to make friends at school.
Group projects are the best way to learn about geography.
People who are quiet usually think they are better than others.
Understanding someone’s situation can turn dislike into kindness.
items.skill: Determines theme in literary text

items.stem: Which is the BEST objective summary of the story?
options: Yusuf moves from Sudan, knows a great deal about the Nile and draws an excellent map for a project about African rivers.
Hassan is an unkind boy who makes fun of a new student because of his accent, and the class teacher should have punished him severely for it.
Hassan dislikes Yusuf until a project reveals that Yusuf is worried about his father, and Hassan then reaches out to him in friendship.
Mr. Saleh gives the class a project on rivers, and Hassan and Yusuf get the best mark because Yusuf knows the Nile well.
items.skill: Writes or identifies an objective summary

passage.title: Saad’s Silence
paras: Every morning at break, the same group of boys gathered by the water fountain, and every morning they found someone to laugh at. This week it was Majed, whose glasses were held together with tape.
“Professor Tape!” Ali called, and the others laughed. Saad laughed too, though not very loudly. He told himself it was only a joke. Majed pushed his glasses up and walked away without a word.

On Thursday, Saad saw Majed sitting alone behind the library, carefully winding new tape around the broken frame. His hands were shaking. Saad wanted to say something, but he did not know what, so he turned around and left.
That night, Saad could not sleep. He kept seeing Majed’s shaking hands. He realised that he had not said a single cruel word, yet his laughter had been part of the cruelty.

On Sunday, when Ali shouted, “Here comes Professor Tape!”, Saad did not laugh. He felt his face grow hot. “Leave him alone,” he said. His voice was quieter than he wanted, but the boys heard it. Ali stared at him, shrugged and turned away.
Later, Saad found Majed in the library. “I’m sorry,” he said. “I laughed when I shouldn’t have.” Majed looked at him for a long moment. Then he moved his bag off the chair beside him.

items.stem: Why does Saad laugh at first, even though he does not shout anything?
options: He tells himself that it is only a harmless joke.
He thinks Majed is laughing at the joke too.
He believes that Majed deserves to be teased by the others.
He wants Ali to choose him as a best friend.
items.skill: Explains character motivation

items.stem: What do Majed’s shaking hands in the third paragraph suggest?
options: He is angry and planning to fight Ali.
He is more hurt by the teasing than he shows.
He is cold because he is sitting outside in the wind.
He is nervous about an exam that day.
items.skill: Determines details that reveal characters’ feelings

items.stem: What does Saad realise in the fourth paragraph?
options: Ali is not really his friend and has been laughing at him as well.
Majed has been teasing other students when the teachers are not looking.
Laughing along made him part of the cruelty, even without cruel words.
He should tell the head teacher about everything he has seen.
items.skill: Analyzes how a character’s thoughts develop

items.stem: “His voice was quieter than he wanted, but the boys heard it.” What does this sentence show?
options: Saad is ill and cannot speak in a loud voice.
The boys are not interested in anything Saad says.
Saad wants to keep his words secret from Majed.
Speaking up is hard for Saad, but he does it anyway.
items.skill: Analyzes how a character responds to challenges

items.stem: What does Majed’s action of moving his bag off the chair show?
options: He is making room for Ali and his friends.
He wants Saad to leave him alone in the library.
He accepts Saad’s apology and invites him to sit.
He is getting ready to leave the library.
items.skill: Makes inferences from literary text

items.stem: Which theme is developed through Saad’s experience?
options: Popular students always decide who is laughed at in class.
Libraries are the safest places in a school to spend break.
Glasses should be repaired properly instead of being taped.
Staying silent while others are hurt is not truly innocent.
items.skill: Analyzes the development of theme in literary text

items.stem: Which is the BEST objective summary of the story?
options: Majed’s glasses are broken, so he spends his breaks in the library fixing them with tape while other boys laugh at him.
Saad laughs when others tease Majed, feels guilty after seeing Majed upset, speaks up against the teasing and apologises.
Ali and his friends tease students every morning until a teacher finally discovers what they are doing and stops them.
Saad is a weak boy who follows the crowd and should have been punished for laughing at a classmate with broken glasses.
items.skill: Writes or identifies an objective summary

passage.title: How Coffee Spread from Yemen
paras: Today, coffee is one of the most popular drinks in the world, and in Saudi Arabia a small cup of *qahwa* is a sign of welcome. Yet coffee drinking has a surprisingly short history compared with tea, and its story begins in the mountains of Yemen.
**From Bean to Drink**

The coffee plant probably grew wild in Ethiopia, across the Red Sea. By the fifteenth century, farmers in Yemen had begun to cultivate it on terraces cut into steep mountainsides. Scholars and worshippers there roasted the beans and boiled them, discovering that the drink helped them stay awake for long nights of study and prayer.
**Across the Region**

Merchants carried coffee north along the trade routes. By the early sixteenth century, it was being drunk in Makkah and Cairo, and by the middle of that century coffee houses had opened in Istanbul. These coffee houses became places to meet, talk and hear the news. Some rulers worried that people gathered there to criticise them, and coffee was even banned for short periods, but the bans never lasted.
**To the World**

For many years, the Yemeni port of Mocha was the centre of the world coffee trade. Later, traders took plants to other parts of the world, where huge plantations were created. Today most coffee comes from countries far from Arabia, but the region’s traditions of preparing and serving coffee remain an important part of daily life and hospitality.

items.stem: What is the central idea of the text?
options: Coffee drinking began in Yemen and spread across the region and then around the world.
Scholars in Yemen roasted coffee beans so that they could sell them to merchants.
Ethiopia grows more coffee today than any other country in the world.
Coffee was banned in many cities because rulers believed it was unhealthy for people.
items.skill: Determines main/central idea in informational text

items.stem: How is the text mainly organized?
options: as a problem followed by several possible solutions
chronologically, following coffee from its beginning to the present
as a list of the steps for preparing coffee in the traditional Arabian way
as a comparison of coffee and tea in many different countries
items.skill: Identifies chronology as a structure

items.stem: According to the text, why did scholars and worshippers in Yemen drink coffee?
options: It was cheaper than tea and easier to carry on long journeys.
It was the only drink that could be made in the mountains.
It was given to them as a gift by merchants from Cairo.
It helped them stay awake for long nights of study and prayer.
items.skill: Locates details in informational text

items.stem: How does the section “Across the Region” contribute to the text?
options: It describes how farmers built terraces to grow coffee on mountainsides.
It shows how the coffee plant first grew wild in the forests of Ethiopia.
It explains how coffee moved to new cities and became part of social life.
It explains why most coffee today is grown in countries far from Arabia.
items.skill: Analyzes how specific sections contribute to meaning

items.stem: Why were some coffee bans put in place, according to the text?
options: Some merchants wanted to raise the price of coffee in the markets.
Some farmers wanted people to drink tea grown in their own fields.
Some doctors warned that coffee caused serious illness in young children.
Some rulers worried that people met in coffee houses to criticise them.
items.skill: Determines the cause of a situation

items.stem: Which sentence would BEST complete a summary of the text?

Coffee is a delicious drink, and everyone should try a cup of qahwa at least once in their lives.

Coffee houses in Istanbul were the best places in the world to hear the news.
items.skill: Summarizes informational text

passage.title: The Great Green Wall
paras: South of the Sahara Desert lies the Sahel, a long belt of dry grassland that stretches across Africa from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea. For decades, droughts, overgrazing and the cutting of trees have damaged the land there, and in many places the desert has advanced.

In 2007, a group of African countries launched an ambitious plan called the **Great Green Wall**. The original idea was to plant a line of trees about 8,000 kilometres long across the continent, like a living barrier against the desert.

Over time, the plan changed. Experts pointed out that a single line of trees would be hard to water and protect. Instead, the project now aims to restore a mosaic of farms, grasslands and woodlands. Local farmers are encouraged to protect young trees that grow naturally from old roots, to build small stone walls that slow rainwater, and to plant crops that hold the soil.

Progress has been slower than hoped. Funding has arrived late, and conflict in some areas has made work difficult. Still, millions of hectares have been restored, and in some villages farmers report better harvests and more water in their wells. Supporters say the project shows that fighting desertification depends as much on people as on trees.

items.stem: What problem is the Great Green Wall meant to address?
options: the floods caused by heavy rain near the Red Sea
the shortage of wood for building houses in Africa
the lack of roads across the Sahara Desert
the spread of desert into damaged land in the Sahel
items.skill: Identifies problem-solution as a structure

items.stem: According to the text, which THREE causes have damaged the land?
options: roads, factories and new cities
droughts, overgrazing and cutting trees
conflict, late funding and slow progress
floods, storms and earthquakes
items.skill: Determines the cause of a situation

items.stem: Why did the plan change from a single line of trees?
options: Experts said such a line would be hard to water and protect.
The trees grew so fast that they blocked the roads.
The countries could not agree on where the line of trees should go.
Farmers refused to allow any trees on their land.
items.skill: Understands explicit relationships between ideas

items.stem: What is the central idea of the text?
options: Farmers in the Sahel have better harvests because rainfall has increased in recent years.
The Great Green Wall has failed completely because there was never enough money to plant and water all of the trees.
The Great Green Wall has changed into a people-centred effort to restore land, with mixed but real results.
The Sahel is a belt of grassland that stretches from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea.
items.skill: Determines main/central idea in informational text

items.stem: What does the word **mosaic** suggest in the third paragraph?
options: a single forest that covers the region
a mixture of many different kinds of land
a wall made of small coloured stones
a picture painted on the side of a village
items.skill: Determines the meaning of a word used figuratively

items.stem: How does the last paragraph contribute to the text?
options: It explains exactly where the Sahel begins and where it ends.
It gives instructions for building stone walls.
It describes the history of the Sahara Desert.
It weighs the project’s difficulties against its successes.
items.skill: Analyzes how specific paragraphs contribute to meaning

items.stem: Which statement would the supporters mentioned in the last sentence MOST LIKELY agree with?

Trees alone are enough to stop the desert from spreading.
Only national governments can solve the problem of desertification.
The project should return to its original single line of trees.
items.skill: Determines author’s or others’ viewpoint

units.title: Words in Context

passage.title: Roots, Clues and Shades of Meaning
paras: Many English words are built from Greek and Latin parts. If you know that **spect** means *look*, you can work out that a **spectator** is someone who watches.
**Context clues** are words nearby that explain a new word. Look for a definition, an example, a contrast (*but, however, unlike*) or a cause (*because, so*).
Words with similar meanings can have different **connotations**, or feelings. *Curious* sounds positive; *nosy* sounds negative.
**Figurative language** says more than the literal words: “The classroom was a furnace” means the room was very hot.

items.stem: The root **port** means “carry.” Goods that a country **exports** are goods that it —
options: sends out to sell in other countries
buys from companies in other countries
keeps in warehouses inside the country
makes in factories for its own people

passage.title: The Last Ferry
paras: I almost missed the last ferry to the Farasan Islands. By the time my uncle and I ran up the ramp, the sun was already sliding toward the horizon, turning the water the colour of copper.

At first the journey was beautiful. Flying fish skimmed beside the boat like silver stones, and the passengers laughed and pointed. But halfway across, the wind changed. The copper sea turned grey, and a long, slow swell began to lift the ferry and drop it again, lift it and drop it.

The laughing stopped. A baby cried somewhere below deck. I gripped the cold rail and watched the lights of Jizan disappear behind us, while ahead there was nothing but gloom. My uncle, who had made this crossing a hundred times, kept talking calmly about the gazelles we would see on the islands, but I noticed that he was holding the rail too.

Then, through the darkness, a single light appeared, then another, then a whole curved line of them. “Farasan,” my uncle said, and his voice sounded lighter. The sea seemed to calm almost at once, though perhaps it was only me.

That night, lying in my bed in my aunt’s house, I could still feel the floor rising and falling. But I also remembered the moment the lights appeared, and I decided that it was the most vivid thing I had ever seen.

items.stem: From which point of view is the story told?
options: first person, by the boy’s uncle
third person, by a narrator who knows only the uncle’s thoughts
third person, by a narrator who knows every passenger’s thoughts
first person, by the boy on the ferry
items.skill: Recognizes first-person point of view

items.stem: How does the mood change between the second and third paragraphs?
options: from cheerful and beautiful to tense and uneasy
from tense and uneasy to cheerful and calm again
from bored and sleepy to excited and curious
from sad and quiet to angry and loud
items.skill: Determines mood in context

items.stem: What does the detail that the uncle “was holding the rail too” suggest?
options: The uncle wanted to show the narrator how to stand safely.
The uncle had never crossed this part of the sea before.
The uncle was also worried, even though he sounded calm.
The uncle was trying to see the gazelles on the islands.
items.skill: Makes inferences from literary text

items.stem: “A long, slow swell began to lift the ferry and drop it again, lift it and drop it.” What is the effect of the repeated words?

They imitate the steady, uncomfortable movement of the boat.
They show that the uncle is repeating the same story.
They show that the narrator cannot remember what happened.
items.skill: Analyzes the effect of repetition and imagery

items.stem: How does the setting affect the narrator?
options: The calm water makes him decide to visit the Farasan Islands every year.
The crowded ferry makes him angry with the passengers who are laughing.
The beautiful sunset makes him forget all about the long and tiring journey that still lies ahead of him.
The dark, rough sea frightens him, which makes the sight of the island lights more powerful.
items.skill: Analyzes how setting affects characters

items.stem: What does the narrator mean by “though perhaps it was only me”?
options: He wonders whether his own relief, not the sea, made the crossing feel calmer.
He thinks that the uncle did not notice the lights of the islands.
He realizes that the storm had been far worse than anyone had said.
He believes that he was the only passenger who stayed out on the deck in the wind.

passage.title: The Old Port
paras: The cranes are tall and silent now,
Their long necks bent above the quay;
Where once a hundred dhows would bow
And sail for India and the sea.
My grandfather can name each one:
The *Pearl*, the *Swift*, the *Morning Star*;
He says their sails could hide the sun,
He says their songs were heard from far.
Now steel ships pass, too big to land,
And no one sings, and no one waits;
But when he takes me by the hand,
The old port opens all its gates.

items.stem: Who is the speaker of the poem?
options: a young person walking with his grandfather
an old sailor remembering his voyages to India
the captain of a modern steel ship
a crane standing above the old port
items.skill: Identifies the speaker in poetry

items.stem: “Their long necks bent above the quay.” What are the “long necks”?
options: the ropes of the steel ships
the necks of seabirds
the masts of the old dhows
the arms of the tall cranes
items.skill: Interprets metaphor in context

items.stem: What contrast does the poem develop?
options: between the speaker’s home in India and his home in Arabia
between the beauty of the steel ships and the ugliness of the dhows
between the busy, lively port of the past and the quiet port of today
between the grandfather’s happiness and the speaker’s sadness
items.skill: Analyzes how specific parts of a poem contribute to meaning

items.stem: What is the mood of the third stanza’s first two lines?
options: frightening and dangerous
empty and a little sad
busy and excited
angry and bitter
items.skill: Determines mood in context

items.stem: “He says their sails could hide the sun.” What kind of language is this?
options: onomatopoeia, imitating the sound of the wind in sails
a fact, describing the size of each sail
hyperbole, to show how many ships there were
a simile, comparing sails to clouds
items.skill: Interprets hyperbole in context

items.stem: What do the final two lines suggest?
options: The grandfather’s memories bring the old port back to life for the speaker.
The speaker and his grandfather plan to sail to India.
The grandfather has the keys to open the old gates of the port at night.
The port will soon be rebuilt for dhows to use again.
items.skill: Analyzes the effect of figurative language

items.stem: What is the theme of the poem?
options: Ports should be kept quiet so that people can rest.
Memories passed between generations keep the past alive.
Steel ships are faster and more useful than wooden dhows.
Old cranes should be removed from modern harbours.
items.skill: Determines theme in poetry

passage.title: Every School Should Teach Cooking
paras: Most students can use a smartphone in seconds, yet many cannot cook a simple, nutritious meal. Every intermediate school should offer a weekly cooking class.
First, cooking is a life skill. Young people who can prepare their own food are more independent and less likely to depend on fast food, which is often high in salt, sugar and fat.
Second, cooking teaches other subjects in a practical way. Measuring ingredients uses fractions, following a recipe develops reading skills, and understanding why bread rises is a science lesson.

Some people argue that schools are already too busy and that cooking should be taught at home. It is true that the timetable is full. However, many families have little time to teach cooking, and one period a week could replace part of a lesson that already covers the same skills, such as practical mathematics.
A student who can cook a healthy meal is ready for life. Isn’t that what school is for?

items.stem: What is the author’s claim?
options: Families should teach their children to cook healthy meals at home.
Every intermediate school should offer a weekly cooking class.
Fast food is high in salt, sugar and fat and should be banned.
Students should spend less time using their smartphones each day.
items.skill: Determines author’s main argument or claim

items.stem: Which reason does the author give in the third paragraph?
options: Cooking makes students more independent and less reliant on fast food.
Cooking classes are cheaper to run than most other school lessons.
Cooking teaches mathematics, reading and science in a practical way.
Cooking helps families spend more time together in the evenings.
items.skill: Identifies reasons that support a claim

items.stem: Which word in the first paragraph creates a contrast to grab the reader’s attention?
options: yet
simple
every
most
items.skill: Analyzes how word choice advances purpose

items.stem: How does the author respond to the counterclaim?
options: by arguing that schools are not busy at all and have plenty of free time for new subjects
by agreeing that cooking should be taught only at home by families
by ignoring the counterclaim and repeating the first reason again
by admitting the timetable is full and suggesting cooking replace part of a related lesson
items.skill: Identifies a counterclaim and rebuttal

items.stem: Which piece of evidence would MOST strengthen the author’s argument?
options: a story about a famous chef who learned to cook as an adult
a study showing that students who take cooking classes eat healthier meals
a list of the most popular fast-food restaurants in the city and their prices
a photograph of a modern school kitchen with new equipment
items.skill: Evaluates evidence used to support claims

items.stem: What is the purpose of the question at the end of the text?
options: to ask readers for information the author does not know
to show that the author is unsure about the claim
to make readers agree by suggesting the answer is obvious
to introduce a new topic that will be discussed later
items.skill: Analyzes persuasive techniques

passage.title: Our City Needs Safe Bicycle Lanes
paras: On cool winter evenings, the streets of our neighbourhood fill with young people on bicycles. But they ride between parked cars and fast traffic, and many parents will not let their children ride at all. The city should build protected bicycle lanes in every neighbourhood.

First, safe lanes would make cycling a real way to travel. A trip of three kilometres to school or the shops takes only about fifteen minutes by bicycle. If students could ride safely, fewer parents would need to drive them, and morning traffic would be lighter.
Second, cycling is good for health. Regular exercise strengthens the heart and helps people manage stress. A lane that makes exercise part of the daily journey could help many families.

Some people say that our summer is far too hot for cycling. This is a fair point: few people will ride at 45 °C. However, the weather is pleasant for many months of the year, and trees planted along the lanes would give shade and make the city greener at the same time.
Finally, cycling is the future, and everybody already agrees that cars are a terrible way to travel.

items.stem: What is the author’s claim?
options: The city should build protected bicycle lanes in every neighbourhood.
Cars should be banned from all streets in the neighbourhood.
Young people should exercise for at least one hour every day.

passage.title: Text 1: The Morning of the Eagles · Text 2: Birds on the Move
paras: **Text 1: The Morning of the Eagles (a narrative)**

My cousin Badr woke me before dawn. “Hurry,” he whispered, “or we will miss them.” We drove to a hill outside the town and waited with his binoculars. For an hour, nothing happened. Then, as the sun warmed the rocks, the sky began to fill. First one eagle, then ten, then more than I could count, circling higher and higher without moving their wings. “They are riding the warm air,” Badr said. “Tomorrow they will be in Africa.” I watched until my neck hurt, and I felt very small and very lucky.
**Text 2: Birds on the Move (an article)**

Every autumn, millions of birds fly south from Europe and Asia to spend the winter in Africa, and every spring they return. Many of them cross the Arabian Peninsula, which lies on one of the world’s great flyways. Large birds such as eagles and storks save energy by soaring on thermals, columns of warm air that rise as the sun heats the ground. Because thermals form only after the land warms up, these birds usually begin flying in the late morning. Scientists count migrating birds to check the health of each species, and many populations of large birds of prey have fallen in recent decades.

paras: **Text 1: The Day the Lights Came On (a memoir told by a grandfather)**

I was nine years old when the electricity reached our village in the mountains. For weeks, men had been raising tall poles along the road. On the evening it was switched on, the whole village gathered in the square. Someone pressed a switch, and a single bulb above the mosque door glowed white. Nobody spoke. An old man near me covered his eyes with his hand, and I thought he was afraid. Later I understood he was crying. He had spent his whole life reading by the light of a kerosene lamp.
**Text 2: Electricity Reaches the Villages (an article)**

In many countries, electricity reached large cities long before it reached rural villages. Building power lines across mountains and deserts is expensive, and each village has few customers. Governments therefore often paid for rural electrification as a public service. The effects were wide-ranging: pumps could lift water from deep wells, refrigerators could keep food and medicine cold, and children could study after dark. In Saudi Arabia, a major expansion of the national electricity network from the 1970s onward brought power to thousands of towns and villages.

passage.title: The Borrowed Book
paras: Faris had borrowed the library’s only copy of *The Atlas of the Seas* for his geography project. It was a heavy book with a cracked blue cover, and the librarian, Mr. Anwar, had handed it over carefully. “It is very old,” he said. “Please bring it back by Thursday.”

On Wednesday evening, Faris could not find it. He searched his bag, his desk and even the car. His little brother had been playing with his school things, and Faris shouted at him until he cried. Then Faris found the atlas exactly where he had left it, under his own bed, with a corner of the cover torn.
He thought about returning it quietly and saying nothing. The tear was small. Mr. Anwar might not notice.

Instead, on Thursday morning, Faris put the book on the desk and pointed to the tear. “I am sorry,” he said. “I was careless. I can pay for a repair.” Mr. Anwar looked at the corner, then at Faris. “Thank you for telling me,” he said. “Most people would not.” He showed Faris how to mend the cover with special tape, and they fixed it together.
That evening, Faris knocked on his brother’s door. He had one more apology to make.

passage.title: Riyadh Gets a Metro
paras: For decades, getting around Riyadh meant one thing: driving. As the city grew to more than seven million people, its roads became some of the busiest in the region. To ease traffic, the city built a metro system, one of the largest projects of its kind in the world.
**A Network Across the City**

The Riyadh Metro opened in stages beginning in late 2024. It has six lines, colour-coded so that passengers can follow them easily, and about 85 stations spread over roughly 176 kilometres. Many sections run underground or on raised tracks above the streets, and the trains are driverless.
**Designed for the Climate**

Because summer temperatures in Riyadh often pass 45 °C, the stations were designed to stay cool. Many have shaded entrances, and some use special glass and building materials that reduce heat from the sun.
**Changing Habits**

Planners hope the metro, together with a large network of buses, will encourage people to leave their cars at home. Fewer cars on the road could mean less traffic, cleaner air and shorter journeys. Whether residents change their habits will become clear over the coming years.

passage.title: The Two Gardeners
paras: A wealthy merchant wanted the finest garden in the city, so he hired two gardeners and gave each of them half of his land. “In one year,” he said, “I will choose the better garden, and its gardener will stay in my service.”
The first gardener bought fully grown flowering bushes from the market and planted them at once. Within a week his half of the garden was bright with colour, and visitors praised it loudly.

The second gardener spent the first months digging channels, mixing the soil with manure and planting young date palms and small fruit trees. For a long time his half looked like nothing but brown earth and thin green sticks. The first gardener laughed at him.
In the heat of summer, the bought bushes, whose roots had never grown deep, began to dry and die. The young palms and trees, drinking from the channels, grew stronger every week.
At the end of the year, the merchant walked through both halves. Then he turned to the second gardener. “A garden,” he said, “is not judged on the day it is planted, but on the day it is tested.”

passage.title: Why Do We Yawn?
paras: Everybody yawns, and so do many animals, from dogs to fish. Yet scientists still do not fully agree on why yawning happens.

For many years, people believed that we yawn because our bodies need more oxygen. However, experiments have not supported this idea. When volunteers breathed air with extra oxygen, they did not yawn less, and when they breathed air with less oxygen, they did not yawn more.

A newer explanation is that yawning helps to cool the brain. A deep yawn draws in a large amount of air and stretches the jaw, which increases blood flow to the head. Some studies have found that people yawn less often when the air around them is very hot, which fits this idea, because hot air could not cool the brain as well.

Yawning is also famously contagious: seeing, hearing or even reading about a yawn can make a person yawn. Some researchers think this may be linked to empathy, our ability to share other people’s feelings, because people often yawn more after seeing family members and friends yawn than after seeing strangers yawn. Have you yawned yet?

passage.title: How a Sandstorm Begins
paras: A sandstorm can turn a bright afternoon into a brown, choking darkness within minutes. But this dramatic event begins with something simple: wind and loose, dry ground.

When the ground is dry and has few plants to hold it in place, strong winds can lift sand and dust from the surface. Heavier grains of sand bounce along close to the ground, while lighter dust particles can be carried high into the air, sometimes thousands of metres up.

Some of the largest storms form when a mass of cold air moves quickly into an area of hot air. The cold air pushes underneath the warm air and forces it upward, creating strong winds along the boundary. In the Arabian Peninsula, sandstorms are most common in spring and early summer, when the ground is very dry and winds are strong.

Sandstorms can close airports and roads, damage crops and make breathing difficult, especially for people with asthma. Weather services now use satellites to track dust clouds and send warnings so that people can stay indoors, close windows and protect their eyes and mouths.

passage.title: The Goal That Did Not Count
paras: With one minute left in the school final, the score was 1–1. Ziyad dribbled past two defenders and shot. The ball hit the post and bounced over the line. The crowd roared. The referee, standing far away, pointed to the centre: goal.
But Ziyad had seen something no one else had. Just before he shot, the ball had touched his hand. It was not deliberate, and it had happened so fast that only he could have noticed.
His teammates lifted him into the air. The opposing goalkeeper, a boy from the neighbouring school, sat on the grass with his head in his hands.

Ziyad’s heart pounded. If he said nothing, his school would win the cup for the first time in ten years. If he spoke, they might lose. He looked at the referee, then at the goalkeeper. Then he walked across the field.
“It touched my hand,” he said.

The referee stared at him for a long moment and then cancelled the goal. The match ended in a draw, and Ziyad’s team lost on penalties. In the changing room, nobody spoke to him. passage.title: Ibn Sina: The Prince of Physicians
paras: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born near Bukhara in Central Asia in 980. By the age of eighteen, he had studied logic, mathematics and medicine, and he was already treating patients.

His most famous work, *The Canon of Medicine*, gathered the medical knowledge of the Greek, Persian and Indian traditions and added his own observations. It described diseases, their symptoms and their treatments in an organised way. Ibn Sina recognised that some diseases could spread from person to person, and he recommended testing new medicines carefully before using them widely.

The *Canon* was translated into Latin in the twelfth century and became a standard medical textbook in European universities for hundreds of years. This is one reason Ibn Sina is sometimes called “the Prince of Physicians.”

passage.title: The Farasan Islands
paras: About forty kilometres off the coast of Jizan, in the southern Red Sea, lie the Farasan Islands, a group of more than eighty islands. Only a few of them are inhabited, and much of the area is a protected nature reserve.
**Wildlife on Land and Sea**

Every year, thousands of migrating birds rest on the islands on their journeys between Europe, Asia and Africa.

passage.title: The Chess Club Election
paras: Everyone expected Waleed to become captain of the chess club. He had won the school tournament two years in a row, and he never let anyone forget it. When the teacher announced the election, Waleed did not even make a speech. “Everyone knows I’m the best,” he said.

The other candidate was Nabil, a quiet boy who had lost to Waleed in both finals. In his speech, Nabil did not talk about winning. He talked about the younger members who were afraid to play because they kept losing. “I want to start a beginners’ table,” he said, “where nobody laughs at a bad move.”
When the votes were counted, Nabil had won by eleven votes to nine. Waleed stared at the board. “But I’m the best player,” he said, almost to himself.
“You are,” said the teacher. “But the captain isn’t chosen for how he plays. He’s chosen for how he helps others play.”

For a week, Waleed stayed away from the club. Then, one afternoon, Nabil found him standing at the door of the classroom. “The beginners’ table needs someone who can explain openings,” Nabil said. “Nobody explains them better than you.” Waleed hesitated. Then he pulled out a chair.

passage.title: The Poet and the Caliph’s Riddle
paras: Long ago, a caliph who loved riddles announced a contest. “I will give a bag of gold,” he declared, “to anyone who can bring me something that is heavier when it is empty than when it is full.”
Merchants arrived with clever boxes and strange jars, but none of them could answer. Scholars argued for days. At last, a poor young poet asked to speak.
“Commander of the Faithful,” he said, “a purse is heavy on the heart when it is empty, and light when it is full.” The court laughed, and even the caliph smiled.

passage.title: Why Teenagers Feel Awake at Midnight
paras: Many parents complain that their teenage children stay up late and are impossible to wake in the morning. It is tempting to blame phones or laziness, but scientists say biology also plays a part.

Every person has a body clock, called a **circadian rhythm**, that controls when we feel sleepy and when we feel alert. One of its signals is a hormone called **melatonin**, which the body releases in the evening to prepare for sleep. During the teenage years, this release often shifts later, sometimes by two hours or more. As a result, many teenagers simply do not feel sleepy until late at night.

At the same time, experts recommend that teenagers sleep eight to ten hours a night. A student who falls asleep at midnight but must wake at 6 a.m. gets only six hours, and the shortfall builds up during the week. Lack of sleep is linked to poorer concentration, worse mood and slower reaction times.

Phones can make the problem worse, because bright screens late at night can delay sleep even further. Experts therefore suggest putting devices away an hour before bed, keeping a regular bedtime even at weekends, and spending time in daylight in the morning to help reset the body clock.

paras: Anas and Iyad were twins, but nobody who knew them confused them for long. Anas was loud and full of ideas; Iyad was quiet and good with his hands. For the regional science fair, they built a water filter from sand, gravel and charcoal. Anas designed the poster. Iyad spent three weekends testing the filter until the dirty water came out clear.

passage.title: Al-Idrisi’s Map of the World
paras: In the twelfth century, King Roger II of Sicily wanted the most accurate description of the world that anyone could produce. He invited a geographer named Muhammad al-Idrisi, who had been born in Ceuta in North Africa and had studied in Córdoba, to his court in Palermo.

Al-Idrisi did not simply copy older maps. For about fifteen years, he gathered information from earlier geographers, compared their works, and questioned travellers, merchants and sailors who passed through Sicily. When reports disagreed, he tried to keep only the information that several sources confirmed.

In 1154, he completed a large book of geography together with a world map. Unlike most maps today, his map placed south at the top. It showed Europe, Asia and North Africa in remarkable detail, with rivers, mountains and cities, though lands far from the trade routes were much less accurate.

Al-Idrisi’s work was copied and studied for centuries. It remains one of the most important examples of how medieval scholars combined careful research with the experience of ordinary travellers to describe the world.

passage.title: Every Student Should Learn First Aid
paras: Imagine a classmate collapses in the playground. The teacher is on the other side of the school. Would you know what to do? For most students, the honest answer is no. Basic first aid should be a required part of the intermediate curriculum.

Some people argue that children are too young for such serious lessons and might panic or make mistakes. However, courses for young people focus on simple, safe actions, and organisations such as the Saudi Red Crescent already run training designed for students.

passage.title: The Machine That Changed Reading
paras: Before the fifteenth century, most books in Europe were copied by hand. A single book could take months to produce, so books were rare and expensive, and few people owned one.

Around 1450, in the German city of Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing press that used **movable type**: small metal letters that could be arranged into lines, inked, pressed onto paper and then rearranged for the next page. Printing with movable type was not entirely new; printers in China and Korea had used it centuries earlier. But Gutenberg’s system, with metal type, oil-based ink and a strong press, made it possible to print many copies quickly.

The results were dramatic. Within fifty years, printing presses were working in hundreds of European towns, and millions of books had been printed. As books became cheaper, more people learned to read. Scientists could share their findings more widely, and new ideas spread faster than ever before.

Not everyone welcomed the change. Some worried that printing would spread errors or dangerous ideas, and that copyists would lose their work. Yet the press could not be stopped, and many historians consider it one of the most important inventions in human history.

passage.title: The Oud Teacher
paras: The first time Nasser heard Ustadh Kamal play the oud, he was ten years old and standing outside a shop in the old market. The music came through the half-open door like water through a crack in a wall, and he stood there until his mother called him three times.

Now, at thirteen, Nasser sat in that same shop every Tuesday afternoon. Ustadh Kamal was nearly blind, and he taught by listening. “Again,” he would say, before Nasser had even finished a phrase. “Your fingers are playing. Your ears are asleep.”

For months, Nasser hated those words. He practised until his fingertips were hard and sore, and still the old man said, “Again.” One evening, frustrated, Nasser played the piece as fast as he could and put the oud down with a bang. “There,” he said. “Every note was correct.”

Ustadh Kamal was silent for a long time. Then he picked up his own oud and played the same piece slowly, so slowly that Nasser could hear the space between each note, the way one note seemed to answer the one before it. When he finished, he said quietly, “Correct is where music begins. It is not where it ends.”
Nasser walked home without speaking. That night, he played the piece once more, very slowly, listening. And for the first time, he heard what had stopped him outside the shop three years before.

passage.title: The Well-Digger
paras: Each word I learn, I dig a little deeper,
Through sand and stone, through grammar, rule and sum;
Some days the ground is hard, the slope is steeper,
Some days I swear the water will not come.
My teacher says: “The well is not for showing.

passage.title: When Arabia Was Green
paras: Today, the Nefud Desert in northern Saudi Arabia is a sea of red sand dunes. It is hard to imagine it as a land of lakes and grasslands. Yet scientists have found strong evidence that this is exactly what it was, many times over the last several hundred thousand years.

The evidence comes from the ground itself. In places, layers of white sediment lie beneath the dunes. These are the dried beds of ancient lakes. Researchers have also found fossils of animals that need plenty of water, including hippopotamuses, as well as stone tools made by early humans who lived beside the lakes.

Why did the climate change so dramatically? Scientists believe that small, regular changes in the Earth’s orbit shifted the paths of monsoon rains. During some periods, the rains moved far enough north to fill lakes and rivers across Arabia. During others, they retreated, and the desert returned.

These “Green Arabia” periods matter for understanding human history. Many researchers think that the wetter phases created routes along which early humans and animals could move between Africa and Asia. The red dunes, it turns out, are only the latest chapter in a much longer story.
